idiom_name: std::unordered_map<std::type_index, std::any> extension map behind a Subject base
implementation_notes: C++ has no way to add a member to an existing class, so the extension store lives in a Subject base that every extensible key abstraction inherits: the base answers getExtension<T>() by looking up a type token in a std::unordered_map and returns std::any_cast<T>(&value) - a pointer that is null when the capability is absent. std::any (C++17; boost::any before that) holds the extension payload, and std::type_index(typeid(T)) is the type-token identity of Gamma's implementation notes. For an extension point that crosses shared-library boundaries, replace the typeid key with an exported tag object, because std::type_info identity is only guaranteed within one program image where RTTI is enabled. Extensions are owned by the subject (unique_ptr payload or a value in the any) and receive a detach/notify hook before destruction.
pitfalls: std::any requires a copy-constructible payload and stores it by value: a non-copyable extension needs a shared_ptr/unique_ptr inside the any, and any_cast<T>(&any) (pointer form) must be used for lookups - the reference form throws std::bad_any_cast instead of reporting absence.

std::type_index identity is per program image: where RTTI is disabled (-fno-rtti) typeid is unavailable altogether, and a plugin compiled separately can produce a different std::type_info for the same type, so cross-module extension points need an exported tag or interface id.

The map is per subject, so an extension table on every object of a large population costs memory and an indirection per lookup; hoist the table into a side structure or make the extension an intrusive member when the type is yours.

Without a destructor hook the subject never learns that an extension is going away, and an extension holding a raw Subject* can fire after the subject is destroyed - define the ownership rule (subject owns the payload) and pass the back-pointer as a reference.

variants.name: Qt per-instance dynamic properties on QObject
variants.implementation_notes: Frameworks that already carry a meta-object system provide the whole dictionary variation: QObject::setProperty(name, value) adds a named attribute to one instance at runtime when no Q_PROPERTY with that name exists, and QObject::property(name) reads it back - per instance, not per class, with the QVariant carrying the extension payload. This is the pattern's registry supplied by the framework: no base class of your own, no type token, but the subject must derive from QObject and the attribute is keyed by a string, so the project needs a naming convention for property names. Use this variant when Qt is already the application framework; use the std::any variant when the subject cannot inherit QObject.
pitfalls: setProperty() returns false both when the value was stored in an existing declared property and when a new dynamic property was created, so the return value cannot be used to detect failure - test property(name).isValid() instead.

Dynamic properties live in the instance's QMetaObject data and are invisible to Q_PROPERTY-based tooling (bindings, designer, moc-generated documentation), so a misspelled name silently creates a second, unused attribute.

Setting an invalid QVariant removes the property and its payload (QVariant must be deleted explicitly for pointer types), and a custom type needs Q_DECLARE_METATYPE or value<T>() cannot recover it - the extension is leaked or lost depending on that registration.
